proposed_derivations.claim:
The bounded Hessian and [F3] imply that $\nabla V$ is globally Lipschitz. Thus $X$ is globally Lipschitz; [F2] gives a unique global flow $\Phi_t$. The bound $|X(z)|\le C(1+|z|)$ follows from this Lipschitz estimate and $X(0)$, so the integral equation and Gronwall bound $\Phi_t(z)$ on each compact time interval and compact initial set. To obtain the smoothness needed below, start with the $C^2$ flow and variational equations of [F1]. Assume inductively that the state derivatives through order $k-1$ are continuous. For a coordinate vector $e_j$, take the difference quotient of the integral equation for $D^{k-1}\Phi_t(z)$ between $z+he_j$ and $z$. The mean-value integral formula applied to each occurrence of $D^\ell X(\Phi_t(z+he_j))-D^\ell X(\Phi_t(z))$ writes this quotient as a linear integral equation whose coefficients converge uniformly on compact time/initial sets, since the lower derivatives of $\Phi$ and the derivatives of $X$ are uniformly continuous on their compact images. The chain rule expresses its limiting inhomogeneous term as
$$ \sum_{\substack{\pi\text{ a partition of }\{1,\ldots,k\}\\|\pi|\ge2}} D^{|\pi|}X(\Phi_t(z)) \big[D^{|B_1|}\Phi_t(z),\ldots,D^{|B_{|\pi|}|}\Phi_t(z)\big], $$
where $B_1,\ldots,B_{|\pi|}$ are the blocks of $\pi$; the unknown $D^k\Phi_t$ appears linearly with coefficient $DX(\Phi_t)$, and its initial value is $0$ for $k\ge2$. The corresponding linear Volterra equation has a unique solution by the same local Picard iteration as [F1], and Gronwall [F7] makes the difference between the quotient and that solution tend uniformly to zero. Thus $D^k\Phi_t$ exists and is continuous, completing the induction. Since $DX$ is bounded and all $D^\ell X$ for $\ell\ge2$ are bounded by the assumed bounds on derivatives of $V$, the variational equation bounds $D\Phi_t$; each higher equation has bounded forcing made from lower derivatives, so induction and Gronwall bound every $D^k\Phi_t$ on compact time/initial sets. Hence $(t,z)\mapsto\Phi_t(z)$ is smooth with all finite derivatives bounded there.

For $b\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^{2d})$, its Weyl kernel is Schwartz in $(x,y)$. Differentiating under its integral and multiplying by powers of $x$ leaves absolutely integrable products of Schwartz functions, so $\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)$ maps $\mathcal S$ into itself. Apply [F5] on $\mathcal S$ to obtain the bounded identity
$$ \frac{i}{\epsilon}[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(b)] =\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(\{b,h\})+\epsilon^2\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,b,V}). $$
The right side is bounded by [F5] and [F6]. Because $\mathcal S$ is a graph core for $H_\epsilon$, this commutator identity extends to $D(H_\epsilon)$: if $u_n\in\mathcal S$, $u_n\to u$, and $H_\epsilon u_n\to H_\epsilon u$, then boundedness of $\operatorname{Op}(b)$ and of the commutator makes both $\operatorname{Op}(b)u_n$ and $H_\epsilon\operatorname{Op}(b)u_n=\operatorname{Op}(b)H_\epsilon u_n+[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}(b)]u_n$ converge; closedness of $H_\epsilon$ gives $\operatorname{Op}(b)u\in D(H_\epsilon)$ and the identity there.

Put $a_s=a\circ\Phi_{t-s}$ for fixed $t$. Since $\Phi_\tau$ is a global diffeomorphism with inverse $\Phi_{-\tau}$, $\operatorname{supp}(a_s)=\Phi_{-(t-s)}(\operatorname{supp}a)$. Since $|t-s|\le2T$, the image of $[-2T,2T]\times\operatorname{supp}a$ under the continuous flow is compact, and step 1.1 bounds all derivatives of $a_s$ on that compact set. Thus $a_s\in C_c^\infty$, its supports lie in one compact set for $|s|,|t|\le T$, and every fixed finite symbol seminorm of $a_s$ is uniformly bounded. To verify the bracket identity, write $X=(\partial_\xi h,-\partial_x h)$, so $Xf=\{f,h\}$. Differentiating the autonomous flow law $\Phi_{\tau+r}(z)=\Phi_\tau(\Phi_r(z))$ in $r$ at $0$ gives $D\Phi_\tau(z)X(z)=X(\Phi_\tau(z))$. The chain rule now gives
$$ \partial_s a_s=-\{a_s,h\}. $$
The family $H_\epsilon/\epsilon$ is constant on the common graph domain $D(H_\epsilon)$, so [F4] supplies the forward propagator for $t\ge0$; its inverse defines $U_\epsilon(t)=U_\epsilon(-t)^*$ for $t<0$. It preserves $D(H_\epsilon)$ and is strongly differentiable there.

For $\psi\in D(H_\epsilon)$, differentiate
$$ F(s)\psi:=U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a_s)U_\epsilon(s)\psi . $$
The domain preservation in [F4] and step 1.2 justify the product rule in $L^2$; the symbol derivative in step 2.1 is also an operator-norm derivative by [F6], since the symbols and their difference quotients have common compact support and converge with all derivatives required by that estimate. The two Hamiltonian terms combine to $U_\epsilon(s)^*(i/\epsilon)[H_\epsilon,\operatorname{Op}(a_s)]U_\epsilon(s)$; $\partial_s\operatorname{Op}(a_s)=-\operatorname{Op}(\{a_s,h\})$ cancels its Poisson term by step 1.2. Therefore
$$ F'(s)\psi=\epsilon^2U_\epsilon(s)^*\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})U_\epsilon(s)\psi . $$
Step 2.1 gives a uniform bound on $p_{12d+16}(a_s)$. The remainder estimate [F5] followed by [F6] consequently yields
$$ \sup_{|s|,|t|\le T}\|\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(r_{\epsilon,a_s,V})\|\le C_{T,V,a}. $$
Integrate the derivative by [F7], use unitarity, and evaluate the endpoints $F(t)\psi=U_\epsilon(t)^*\operatorname{Op}(a)U_\epsilon(t)\psi$ and $F(0)\psi=\operatorname{Op}(a\circ\Phi_t)\psi$. This gives the required $C_{T,V,a}|t|\epsilon^2\|\psi\|$ bound on the dense domain; boundedness of both endpoint operators extends it to all of $L^2$, uniformly for $|t|\le T$. Reversing the integration orientation gives the same estimate for $t<0$.

If $V$ has degree at most two, then $D^3V=0$, so the integral Taylor remainder $\Delta_V$ in the proof of [[lem-nrqmx-cubic-moyal-commutator-remainder]] vanishes. The identity in step 1.2 then has no $\epsilon^2$ term; the derivative in step 3.1 is identically zero, and the two endpoint operators are equal for every $t$.

proposed_derivations.claim:
The scaled oscillator eigenfunctions are polynomial multiples of $e^{-x^2/(2\epsilon)}$. To verify the core hypothesis of [[thm-nrqmx-quadratic-egorov]], take $f\in\mathcal S(\mathbb R)$ and set $L f=-\epsilon^2f''/2+x^2f/2\in L^2$. Integration by parts against each Hermite eigenfunction $\psi_n^\epsilon$, whose polynomial-Gaussian tails make the endpoint products vanish, gives
$$ \langle Lf,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\langle f,L\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle =\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle. $$
Parseval for the complete basis [F1] yields
$$ \sum_{n\ge0}\epsilon^2(n+\tfrac12)^2|\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle|^2 =\|Lf\|_2^2<\infty. $$
Thus $f\in D(H_\epsilon)$. The coefficients of $H_\epsilon f$ in the Hermite basis are $\epsilon(n+\tfrac12)\langle f,\psi_n^\epsilon\rangle$, the same coefficients as $Lf$; completeness of that basis gives $H_\epsilon f=Lf$. The finite Hermite span is contained in $\mathcal S$ and is a graph core by [F1]; since $\mathcal S\subset D(H_\epsilon)$, $\mathcal S$ is also a core. This checks every operator hypothesis of [F4].

The Gaussian integral [F5] gives $\|\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\|_2^2=(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2}\int e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon}dx=1$. In its Wigner integral, the product of the two Gaussian factors is
$$ (\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} \exp\!\left(-\frac{(x-q)^2}{\epsilon}-\frac{y^2}{4\epsilon}\right) \exp\!\left(\frac{ipy}{\epsilon}\right). $$
Multiplying by $e^{-iy\xi/\epsilon}$ and applying [F3] with $\eta=\xi-p$ gives
$$ W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](x,\xi) =(2\pi\epsilon)^{-1}(\pi\epsilon)^{-1/2} e^{-(x-q)^2/\epsilon} 2\sqrt{\pi\epsilon}\,e^{-(\xi-p)^2/\epsilon}, $$
which is the stated normalized density. Each centered coordinate has an even Gaussian factor, so its mean and the cross-covariance vanish; each coordinate variance is $\epsilon/2$ by one Gaussian second-moment integration by parts as in [F5]. Thus its covariance is $(\epsilon/2)I_2$.

The classical Hamilton equations for $h(x,\xi)=(x^2+\xi^2)/2$ solve to
$$ \Phi_t(x,\xi)=(x\cos t+\xi\sin t,\ \xi\cos t-x\sin t). $$
This matrix is orthogonal with determinant $1$, and $\Phi_t(q,p)=(q_t,p_t)$. For $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^2)$, [F4] gives
$$ \langle W_t,a\rangle =\langle\operatorname{Op}^W_\epsilon(a\circ\Phi_t)\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}, \psi^\epsilon_{q,p}\rangle =\int_{\mathbb R^2}a(\Phi_t z)W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](z)\,dz, $$
where the last equality is [F2]. Change variables $z'=\Phi_tz$; determinant $1$ gives density $W_\epsilon[\psi^\epsilon_{q,p}](\Phi_{-t}z')$. Orthogonality gives
$$ |\Phi_{-t}(x,\xi)-(q,p)|^2 =|(x,\xi)-\Phi_t(q,p)|^2, $$
so this density is exactly the displayed $W_t$. This orthogonal rotation preserves the covariance $(\epsilon/2)I_2$. This proves the asserted exact transport for every compactly supported smooth test symbol and hence for the distributional Wigner functional defined in the Statement.

proposed_derivations.claim: The matrix $k$ is unitary and has determinant $i(-i)=1$, so $k\in SU(2)$; also $k\ne I_2$ and $k^{-1}\ne I_2$. By [F1], $g'_{e_1}=I_2I_2k^{-1}=k^{-1}$, $g'_{e_2}=I_2$, and $g'_{e_3}=kI_2I_2=k$. Thus individual edge matrices change.

Their later-left loop product is $g'_{e_3}g'_{e_2}g'_{e_1}=kI_2k^{-1}=I_2$, whose defining-representation trace is $2$. The original product is also $I_2$ and has trace $2$; this concrete calculation agrees with [F2].

proposed_derivations.claim:
Since $E_0>0$, $e\ne0$, and direct calculation gives
$k\cdot e=0$, $k\times e/\omega=(E_0/c)e_2=b$, and $\omega=c|k|$.
Therefore [F3] gives a smooth source-free Maxwell solution and [F1] makes it
nonzero. By [F2], its period-averaged energy density is
$\varepsilon_0E_0^2/2>0$ and its total energy over $\mathbb R^3$ is infinite.

Every member of the Fourier-packet domain in [F4] has finite energy.
Thus the nonzero wave of step 1.1 does not belong to that domain, refuting the
universal statement. Componentwise formal cancellations do not make these
all-space functionals defined on this field.
